questions.prompt: A new drug blocks reverse transcriptase. Why would it stop new HIV infections of cells but not cure cells that are already infected?

options.text: It blocks membrane fusion, which already-infected cells no longer need, so they keep making virus
It blocks RNA → DNA conversion in newly entered virions, but cells that already carry a provirus can keep transcribing it into new viral RNA
It destroys the provirus in infected cells, but it can't get into uninfected cells to protect them
It blocks budding, which only happens in newly infected cells, so older infected cells keep releasing virus

questions.explanation: Reverse transcription happens right after uncoating. Once the dsDNA is in the chromosome, the provirus is the template — no reverse transcriptase needed.

questions.prompt: If one normal cell divided 50 times and every daughter cell survived and also divided, about how many cells would result?

options.text: About 10^15 (2^50 ≈ 1.1 quadrillion)
About 100 (two new cells from each of the 50 divisions)
About 10^6 (one million, the size of a small tumor)
About 2,500 (50 cells, each dividing 50 times)

questions.explanation: Each division doubles the count: 2^50 ≈ 1.1 × 10^15. Normal biopsy cells stop after about 50 divisions; HeLa cells never stop.

questions.prompt: A newly discovered human virus infects only one type of human liver cell. Which culture method from the course would most likely be needed?

options.text: Bacterial cultures in solid or liquid media, as with phages, since bacteria are easy to grow
Plain nutrient agar, since viruses grow on any rich medium once they are in a lab
Cultures of that specific human cell type, as with HIV — costly and time-consuming
Embryonated eggs, as with influenza, since eggs are cheap and support most viruses

questions.explanation: Viruses only grow in living cells; a narrow host range means you must grow the specific cells it infects.

questions.prompt: Why was filtering the ground-up tumor essential to Rous's conclusion that a virus caused the sarcoma?

options.text: The filter removed the cells, so the new tumor couldn't have come from transplanted cancer cells — the cause had to be something smaller
The filter concentrated the cancer cells, so the injection held enough of them to start a new tumor
The filter removed the sand, which would otherwise have irritated the muscle and caused the tumor
The filter trapped the virus, and the bacteria that passed through were shown to cause the sarcoma

questions.explanation: A cell-free filtrate causing cancer means the agent passed through a filter that traps cells — a virus.

questions.prompt: Why must HIV cultures of human cells be passaged (moved to fresh cultures) again and again?

options.text: Passaging removes the egg proteins that would otherwise block HIV from entering
The cells turn into immortal HeLa-like cells unless they are moved to new dishes
HIV only grows in cells younger than one day, so fresh cells are added each morning
The viruses destroy the cells while replicating, so new cells are needed to keep the culture going

questions.explanation: Lecture: you have to passage the cells from generation to generation because the viruses destroy them in the process of replicating.

questions.prompt: When culturing viruses in embryonated eggs, why might different viruses be injected at different marked spots?

options.text: Viruses must always be injected away from the embryo so the embryo isn't infected
Each spot is for a different dose of the same virus
The marks show where the egg-allergy proteins collect, so they can be avoided
Different viruses grow best in different regions — the amniotic fluid, the embryo itself, or the yolk sac

questions.explanation: Injection sites include the amniotic fluid, the embryo, or the yolk sac, depending on where the virus grows best.

questions.prompt: Why did signing away rights to her biopsy seem routine for Henrietta Lacks at the time?

options.text: Immortal cell lines had already been grown from many other patients' biopsies
Biopsy samples were normally just used for a diagnosis and then incinerated
Hospitals routinely sold biopsy samples to drug companies, and patients expected it
She had been told her cells would be used to make a cervical cancer vaccine

questions.explanation: Lecture: normally a biopsy is diagnosed and then the cells are destroyed — but her cells 'took a life of their own on.'

questions.prompt: Cats get FIV, which replicates like HIV. Combining Modules 16 and 17, which statement is correct?

options.text: FIV is a dsDNA virus that can infect both cats and humans who handle infected cats
FIV is a retrovirus using reverse transcriptase like HIV, but its narrow host range keeps it from infecting humans
FIV and HIV are the same virus, adapted to the different body temperatures of cats and humans
FIV is a −ssRNA virus, so unlike HIV it never forms a provirus in the cat's cells

questions.explanation: Immunodeficiency viruses are retroviruses (FIV for cats, SIV for monkeys, HIV for humans); each has its own narrow host range.

questions.prompt: Suppose the naked +ssRNA genome of a coronavirus (no capsid, no envelope) were injected straight into a host cell's cytoplasm. Could it start an infection?

options.text: No — + sense RNA must first be reverse-transcribed into DNA, and the virion's enzyme was left behind
No — without its spike proteins attached, the genome can't be transcribed or translated by the host
Yes — ribosomes can translate + sense RNA directly, including the gene for the polymerase that copies the genome
No — + sense RNA can't be read by ribosomes until it is copied into − sense by an enzyme in the capsid

questions.explanation: +ssRNA is 'sense' RNA: it can be directly translated into protein. The host makes the viral polymerase from it and copying begins.

questions.prompt: About how many years passed between Rous linking a virus to cancer in chickens (1911) and Epstein and Barr linking a virus to human cancer (around 1964)?

options.text: About 53 years
About 23 years
About 73 years
About 13 years

questions.prompt: Which statement about culturing viruses is FALSE?

options.text: Growing viruses in animals like mice raises cost and ethical concerns.
People with egg allergies are asked about them before a flu shot because the vaccine virus is grown in eggs.
Bacteriophages can only be grown in liquid cultures.
Viruses of eukaryotic cells can be grown in live animals, embryonated eggs, or cell cultures.
Viruses will only grow in living cells.

questions.explanation: False — phages can be grown easily in bacterial cultures, both solid and liquid.

questions.prompt: Which statement about HPV and cervical cancer is FALSE?

options.text: HPV papillomas on the cervix always turn into cancer.
The cervix is a sphincter between the vagina and the uterus.
As tumors advance they grow their own blood vessels, which causes bleeding.
HPV makes a protein that inactivates p53.
Cervical cancer caught early is very treatable.

questions.explanation: False — papillomas are often harmless; an HPV infection can lead to cancer but doesn't always.

questions.prompt: Which statement about viral biosynthesis is FALSE?

options.text: A −ssRNA genome must be copied into + sense before it can be translated.
A dsDNA virus needs reverse transcriptase to make its mRNA.
A retrovirus's dsDNA copy becomes a provirus in the host chromosome.
Whether making proteins or copying the genome, a template is always required.
A +ssRNA genome can be translated directly by ribosomes.

questions.explanation: False — a dsDNA virus uses ordinary transcription. Reverse transcriptase belongs to retroviruses.

questions.prompt: A lab needs to culture three viruses: a bacteriophage, influenza (for a vaccine), and HIV. Describe the best method for each and explain why.
questions.explanation: All viruses only grow inside living cells. Bacteriophage: grow it in a bacterial culture (solid or liquid), since bacteria are easy and cheap to culture. Influenza: inject it into embryonated (fertilized) eggs — a cheap, self-contained, easily disposed of system; flu grows very well in eggs, which is why people are asked about egg allergies before a flu shot. HIV: it has a narrow host range (CD4+ helper T cells), so the lab must culture those specific human cells, passaging them repeatedly because the virus destroys them — costly and time-consuming. Live animals are another option for some viruses but bring cost, mess, and ethical concerns.

questions.prompt: Compare the filtrate experiments of Ivanovsky, d'Hérelle, and Rous. For each, give the starting material, what the filtrate did, and what it showed.
questions.explanation: Ivanovsky (1892): ground-up diseased tobacco plants passed through a filter that traps bacteria; the cell-free filtrate gave healthy plants tobacco mosaic disease — the first 'filterable infectious poison' (virus). d'Hérelle (1916): a culture of dying bacteria passed through a filter; the filtrate killed bacteria in fresh cultures, making plaques — he discovered bacteriophage (and went on to phage therapy). Rous (1911): chicken sarcoma tissue ground with sand and filtered; the cell-free filtrate caused sarcoma in young chickens — the first link between a virus and cancer (Rous sarcoma virus; Nobel 1966). In all three, something smaller than a cell passed through the filter and caused the effect.
